newsitem.title: UK: OPTIONS - OTC investors hedge high-yield bond bets.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - OTC investors hedge high-yield bond bets.

text.p: Investors are beginning to buy protection in the options market from any year-end retreats in high-yield debt markets after the stratospheric gains they have shown throughout the year, OTC dealers said on Tuesday.

Put buying and call selling have been the order of the day for sectors such as Italian BTPs or Spanish Bonos, they said. But these markets still stand a chance of outperforming core European bonds and options strategies should reflect this.

"We've been recommending to clients that they put on hedging positions on the high yielding markets, especially Spain and Italy," said Robert Coughlan, options specialist at Paribas Capital Markets in London.
He said that as year-end approaches, investors should buy puts on Italy but can finance that by selling puts on Bunds.
"The only real flows that are coming through are put spread buying and call selling (in Italy)," said a dealer at a bank in Paris. "There are a lot of call sellers coming out of the woodwork."
That trend was reinforced by the performance in the Italian BTP futures market this week, traders said.
December BTP futures rose to 124.35 on Monday -- within two basis points of the record 124.37 set on October 9 -- but by 1415 GMT they were down to 122.90, off 0.35 on the day.
Although bearish directional trades were being put on, options strategies that take advantage of any outperformance by high-yielders were still popular, they said.
"Convergence trades continue to be played, where people buy calls on the high yielders, calls on markets such as Denmark, and sell calls on France and Germany," the Paris dealer said.
He said from a longer-term perspective such strategies based on calls were probably better than those based on puts.
"Call-to-call trades are the majority. Whichever way you look at it, the market is expected to remain bullish," he said. "Until the trend changes you can't really go against it."
The trader singled out Denmark as a good market to be long of against Germany. "Denmark has one of the steepest yield curves at the moment. So if you buy a call on Denmark you've got greater carry."
Danish one-month price volatility on 10-year bonds was quoted around 5.6 percent.
Meanwhile, this week's barrage of U.S. economic data was keeping options dealers on their toes and analysts said that would keep U.S. volatilities well-bid through Friday.
One-month price volatility on U.S. 10-year paper was quoted around 8.1 percent, above the 7.8/7.9 percent quotes for three-month vols, traders said.
"Vol in the U.S. market is probably going to climb higher coming up to Friday," Coughlan said.
"The Street is actually looking to buy one month vol and sell one and a half month vol," he said, on the view one month would include the next Federal Open Market Committee meeting.
The trader at the Paris bank said the U.S. backdrop was supporting European vols even though many European countries have a holiday on Friday.
